text: Koshary (also spelled Koshari or Kushari) is the national dish of Egypt. It is a popular street food made of a mixture of lentils, rice, macaroni, and chickpeas, topped with a spicy tomato sauce (tomat) and a garlic-vinegar dressing (da'ah), and garnished with crispy fried onions. It originated in the mid-19th century, drawing influences from Italian, Indian, and Middle Eastern cuisines.

To make traditional Egyptian Koshary, you need: 1 cup brown lentils, 1 cup medium-grain white rice, 1 cup elbow macaroni, 1 cup spaghetti broken into small pieces, 1 can chickpeas (drained), 2 large onions (sliced into thin rings for frying), vegetable oil, 2 cups tomato passata, 4 cloves garlic, 2 tbsp white vinegar, 1 tsp cumin, 1 tsp coriander, chili powder, salt, and pepper. The lentils and rice are typically cooked with cumin, pasta is boiled separately, onion rings are deep-fried until dark brown and crispy, and a tomato sauce is simmered with garlic, vinegar, and spices.

Molokhia (Jute leaves) is a highly popular Egyptian soup. It is made by finely mincing fresh jute leaves and cooking them in a rich meat broth (traditionally rabbit, chicken, or beef) seasoned with spices. The hallmark of a great Molokhia is the 'Ta'leya' - a sizzling mixture of ground coriander and minced garlic fried in ghee, stirred into the soup at the very end of cooking, often accompanied by the famous culinary tradition of 'the gasp' (shah'et el-molokhia) for good luck.

Ful Medames is a cornerstone of the Egyptian diet, traditionally eaten for breakfast. It consists of slow-cooked fava beans, typically stewed overnight in a pot called a 'demesa'. It is served mashed or semi-mashed, dressed with olive oil, flaxseed oil, or butter, and seasoned with cumin, lemon juice, garlic, and salt. It is commonly eaten with warm Egyptian Baladi flatbread, boiled eggs, cheese, and green onions.

Mahshi (meaning 'stuffed') is a beloved Egyptian family meal, especially on Fridays. It involves stuffing vegetables like zucchini, eggplants, bell peppers, tomatoes, cabbage leaves, or grape leaves (Mahshi Wara' Enab) with a savory mixture of short-grain rice, finely chopped dill, parsley, cilantro, tomato paste, grated onions, and spices. The stuffed vegetables are then arranged tightly in a pot, covered with seasoned chicken or beef broth, and simmered until the rice is fully cooked and tender.

Hawawshi is a classic Egyptian meat pie. It consists of spiced minced beef, onions, bell peppers, chilies, and herbs stuffed inside a pocket of Egyptian Baladi flatbread. The bread is brushed with oil or butter and baked in an oven or grilled over charcoal until the bread is crispy and golden and the meat inside is fully cooked. It is typically served with pickled vegetables (Torshi) and Tahini dip.

Umm Ali (meaning 'Mother of Ali') is a traditional Egyptian bread pudding dessert. It dates back to the Ayyubid era. It is made by baking layers of puff pastry, phyllo dough, or croissants mixed with sugar, milk, whipped cream, and a generous assortment of nuts (pistachios, almonds, walnuts), raisins, and shredded coconut until golden brown on top and bubbly.

Egyptian Baladi Bread (Aish Baladi) is a flatbread made of whole wheat flour, bran, water, yeast, and salt. It is baked at extremely high temperatures, causing it to puff up and form a pocket. The word 'Aish' in Egyptian Arabic means 'life', highlighting the bread's vital status as a daily staple in Egyptian culture.

Ta'ameya (Egyptian Falafel) is uniquely made using ground fava beans (broad beans) instead of chickpeas, which are commonly used in other parts of the Middle East. The split fava beans are soaked and blended with fresh leek, green onions, coriander, parsley, garlic, and spices. The mixture is shaped into patties, coated with sesame seeds, and deep-fried until dark green inside and golden-brown crispy on the outside. It is lighter and fluffier than chickpea falafel.

Egyptian Fatteh is a celebratory dish typically served during Islamic festivals like Eid al-Adha. It is constructed in layers starting with a base of crispy toasted Baladi bread pieces, followed by a layer of white medium-grain rice. It is drenched in a hot garlic-vinegar soup/broth and topped with slow-boiled beef or lamb chunks. A final splash of red garlic-vinegar tomato sauce completes the dish.

Mesaqa'ah (Egyptian Musakka) is a baked dish made of layers of sliced fried eggplants, bell peppers, and occasionally sliced potatoes. These layers are bathed in a spiced tomato sauce seasoned with garlic, vinegar, and ground cumin. In many households, a middle layer of spiced minced beef (lahma mafrooma) is added before baking it in the oven until bubbling and browned.

Roz Bel Laban is a traditional Egyptian Rice Pudding. It is made by cooking rice in whole milk, sugar, and cream (qashta), and flavored with vanilla or mastic (mastika) resin. It is cooked slowly until thick and creamy, then cooled in bowls. It is often garnished with a combination of cinnamon, raisins, coconut flakes, and chopped nuts like pistachios.

Basbousa is a traditional Egyptian semolina cake. It is prepared by mixing semolina flour, butter, sugar, yogurt, and sometimes unsweetened coconut. Once baked, the hot cake is instantly drenched in a hot sweet syrup flavored with rosewater or lemon juice, ensuring a moist and soft texture. It is traditionally decorated with blanched almonds or hazelnuts.

Feteer Meshaltet is a flaky, layered Egyptian pastry. The dough is stretched paper-thin, brushed heavily with ghee or butter, and folded repeatedly to create hundreds of delicate layers. It is baked in a very hot oven until it puffs up. It can be served plain, sweet (with powdered sugar or honey), or savory (with cheese, molasses, or old Egyptian salty cheese known as Mish).

Bamia (Egyptian Okra Stew) is a comforting stew made of fresh, small okra pods cooked in a rich, garlicky tomato sauce. It is seasoned with cumin, coriander, and fresh lemon juice. Bamia is often prepared with tender chunks of lamb or beef and is traditionally eaten alongside white rice or scooped up with fresh Baladi bread.

Kabab and Kofta are classic Egyptian charcoal-grilled meats. Kabab consists of marinated cubes of lamb or veal, while Kofta is made of minced lamb or beef mixed with grated onion, parsley, and spices, shaped onto skewers. They are grilled over hot coals and served over a bed of fresh parsley, accompanied by Tahini, Baladi bread, and green salad.

Hamam Mahshi (Stuffed Pigeon) is an Egyptian delicacy reserved for special occasions and weddings. Pigeons are stuffed with a mixture of spiced cracked green wheat (Freekeh) or rice cooked with onions, cinnamon, and nutmeg. The stuffed pigeons are first boiled until cooked, then pan-fried in ghee until golden brown and crispy.

Besara is a cold vegetarian dip made from dried split fava beans cooked with fresh herbs (dill, cilantro, parsley), onions, garlic, and dried mint. Once the beans are tender, they are blended into a thick green paste. The dip is poured into plates and topped with caramelized fried onions. It is eaten cold with Baladi bread.

Sayadeya is a classic coastal Egyptian dish, particularly famous in Alexandria, Suez, and Port Said. It consists of white fish (like sea bass or tilapia) cooked in a spiced brown sauce made from caramelized onions, tomato paste, cumin, and spices. It is served with Sayadeya rice, which is rice cooked in the caramelized onion broth to give it a dark brown color and deep savory flavor.

Shakshouka is a popular breakfast dish in Egypt. It features eggs poached in a flavorful, bubbling sauce of tomatoes, onions, bell peppers, garlic, and spices like cumin and paprika. Fresh herbs like cilantro or parsley are sprinkled on top, and it is served hot straight from the skillet with warm Baladi bread.

Feseekh is a traditional, festive Egyptian fish dish eaten during the spring celebration of Sham El-Nessim. It is made of raw grey mullet fish that has been dried in the sun, salted, and fermented in wooden barrels for several weeks. Because of its intense aroma and salty taste, it is eaten with green onions, fresh lemons, and Baladi bread to balance the flavor.

Renga is smoked herring, commonly eaten during celebrations like Sham El-Nessim alongside Feseekh. Unlike Feseekh, Renga is smoked rather than fermented, offering a smoky-salty flavor. It is often shredded and prepared as a salad mixed with tahini, olive oil, lemon juice, diced tomatoes, cucumbers, and spring onions.
